rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rāzī explains the singular “magician” generically: the wording concerns the class, not a number of individual magicians.
rows.anchor: لأن القصد في هذا الكلام إلى معنى الجنسية لا إلى معنى العدد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The indefinite first mention makes the magicians' work one kind of magic; the definite second mention generalizes the futility to every kind, which is more emphatic.
rows.anchor: هذا الذي أتوا به قسم واحد من أقسام السحر وجميع أقسام السحر لا فائدة فيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rāzī raises the inference that magic cannot attain any aim, good or evil, so the verse seems to deny magic altogether; he refers readers to his earlier discussion of magic in al-Baqara.
rows.anchor: وذلك يقتضي نفي السحر بالكلية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: To block Pharaoh's claim that “Lord of the worlds” meant himself, the magicians named Aaron before Moses: Pharaoh claimed to have raised Moses and thus to be his lord.
rows.anchor: لأن فرعون كان يدعي ربوبيته لموسى بناء على أنه رباه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The magicians had seen God favor Aaron and Moses with great miracles and high ranks, so they confessed to the Lord of both.
rows.anchor: لما شاهدوا أن الله تعالى خصهما بتلك المعجزات العظيمة والدرجات الشريفة لا جرم قالوا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Seeing their prostration and confession, Pharaoh feared that others would imitate them and believe in God and His messenger.
rows.anchor: ثم إن فرعون لما شاهد منهم السجود والإقرار خاف أن يصير ذلك سببا لاقتداء سائر الناس بهم

words: ءَامَنتُمْ لَهُۥ قَبْلَ أَنْ ءَاذَنَ لَكُمْ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Pharaoh's first insinuation was that immediate belief without investigation, debate, or deliberation could not be considered insight-based and must have another cause.
rows.anchor: الاعتماد على الخاطر الأول غير جائز بل لا بد فيه من البحث والمناظرة والاستعانة بالخواطر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Pharaoh's second insinuation was that the magicians were Moses' pupils and had agreed to feign defeat to promote and glorify him.
rows.anchor: يعني أنكم تلامذته في السحر فاصطلحتم على أن تظهروا العجز من أنفسكم ترويجا لأمره وتفخيما لشأنه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After casting doubt on them, Pharaoh threatened them to deter them and to discourage others from following their example of belief.
rows.anchor: ثم بعد إيراد الشبهة اشتغل بالتهديد تنفيرا لهم عن الإيمان وتنفيرا لغيرهم عن الاقتداء بهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rāzī notes an unnamed reading that lightens the forms of both “I will cut off” and “I will crucify.”
rows.anchor: قرىء لأقطعن ولأصلبن بالتخفيف . والقطع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Cutting crosswise means cutting the right hand and left foot, since each is opposite the other in limb and side.
rows.anchor: والقطع من خلاف أن تقطع اليد اليمنى والرجل اليسرى لأن كل واحد من العضوين خلاف الآخر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Crosswise” is accusative as a circumstantial qualifier: the limbs are to be cut in differing ways.
rows.anchor: في محل النصب على الحال أي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The preposition “in” depicts the crucified person as lodged in a trunk like something enclosed in its container; the popular gloss “on the trunks” is weak.
rows.anchor: فشبه تمكن المصلوب في الجذع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: By “which of us,” Pharaoh meant himself and Moses, boasting of his power and habitual cruelty while mocking Moses, who had never tortured anyone.
rows.anchor: يشعر بأنه أراد نفسه وموسى عليه السلام بدليل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although Pharaoh had recently seen the staff become a terrifying serpent and sought Moses' help, Rāzī says Pharaoh may have been inwardly terrified while feigning boldness to preserve his rule; helpless people sometimes act this way.
rows.anchor: قلنا لم لا يجوز أن يقال : إنه كان في أشد الخوف في قلبه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rāzī cites Pharaoh's denial that God's punishment exceeds human punishment and his knowingly false claim about Moses teaching the magicians as evidence of calculated public bravado.
rows.anchor: ومما يدل على صحة ذلك أن كل عاقل يعلم بالضرورة

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says the magicians were magicians at the start of the day and martyrs by its end.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس رضي الله عنهما : ( كانوا في أول النهار سحرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rāzī reports the critics' first dilemma: if Moses ordered Aaron to follow, either Moses sinned by reproaching an innocent follower or Aaron sinned by disobeying; without an order, Moses sinned by reproaching him.
rows.anchor: أحدها : أن موسى عليه السلام إما أن يكون قد أمر هرون باتباعه أو لم يأمره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The critics' second argument is that Moses' rejecting question implies Aaron disobeyed blameworthily; otherwise Moses would have lied, also a sin.
rows.anchor: استفهام على سبيل الإنكار فوجب أن يكون هارون قد عصاه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The critics' third argument treats Moses' seizure of Aaron as sinful whether it occurred before or after Moses learned that Aaron had done all he could to advise and restrain the people.
rows.anchor: وهذا معصية لأن هارون عليه السلام قد فعل ما قدر عليه من النصيحة والوعظ والزجر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The critics' fourth dilemma is that if taking Aaron by the beard and head was permissible, Aaron sinned by forbidding it; if impermissible, Moses sinned by doing it.
rows.anchor: فإن كان الأخذ بلحيته وبرأسه جائزا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rāzī rejects charging prophets with sin from these apparent readings: his earlier proof at 2:36 establishes their immunity, and ambiguous wording cannot override evidence that admits no ready reinterpretation.
rows.anchor: أنا بينا في سورة البقرة في تفسير قوله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: For his first answer, Rāzī notes agreement that prophets may leave what is best: Moses and Aaron could differ over which of two actions was preferable without either sinning.
rows.anchor: أنا وإن اختلفنا في جواز المعصية على الأنبياء لكن اتفقنا على جواز ترك الأولى عليهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An objection says this reading fails because both brothers were decisive in what they did or omitted, whereas recommended acts and omissions do not carry such decisiveness.
rows.anchor: فإن قيل هذا التأويل غير جائز لأن كل واحد منهما كان جازما فيما يأتي به فعلا كان أو تركا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rāzī answers that evidence may qualify an unqualified instruction: they could understand decisiveness as “do or omit this if you seek what is best,” leaving the condition unstated because their agreement on it was established.
rows.anchor: تقييد المطلق بالدليل غير ممتنع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses, angry and thoughtful, may have seized and pulled Aaron as a person might bite his lip, twist his fingers, or grasp his own beard; he treated his brother and partner as himself.
rows.anchor: فأخذ برأس أخيه وجره إليه كما يفعل الإنسان بنفسه مثل ذلك عند الغضب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Aaron's plea can mean he feared suspicious Israelites would misread Moses' gesture as reproach or lack of support, so he asked him not to give them that impression.
rows.anchor: فلا يمتنع أن يكون هرون عليه السلام خاف من أن يتوهم بنو إسرائيل من سوء ظنهم

words: إِنِّى خَشِيتُ أَن تَقُولَ فَرَّقْتَ بَيْنَ بَنِىٓ إِسْرَٰٓءِيلَ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rāzī adds that Israelites were so suspicious they accused Moses of killing Aaron during an absence; after Moses' thirty nights became forty and he returned with the Tablets, he pulled Aaron close to investigate, while Aaron feared baseless suspicion.
rows.anchor: حتى أن هارون غاب عنهم غيبة

rows.speaker: صاحب الكشاف
rows.claim: The author of al-Kashshāf attributes the act to Moses' naturally fierce, rough temper and intense anger for God: stunned at calf worship, he threw the Tablets and confronted Aaron as an enemy.
rows.anchor: كان موسى عليه السلام رجلا حديدا مجبولا على الحدة والخشونة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rāzī rejects al-Kashshāf's anger defense: if Moses remained rational and accountable, the objections remain and anger adds a sin; if not accountable, a Muslim cannot accept that.
rows.anchor: واعلم أن هذا الجواب ساقط لأنه يقال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rāzī says these replies address those who disallow minor sins; for theologians who allow minor sins, the objection no longer stands.
rows.anchor: فهذه أجوبة من لم يجوز الصغائر وأما من جوزها فلا شك في سقوط السؤال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One parsing takes “lā” as extra, yielding “what prevented you from following me?”
rows.anchor: أن لا صلة والمراد ما منعك أن تتبعني

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A second parsing means “what prompted you not to follow me?”; it uses “prevented” in the sense of “prompted.”
rows.anchor: أن يكون المراد ما دعاك إلى أن لا تتبعني

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: In ʿAṭāʾ's transmission from Ibn ʿAbbās, following Moses meant taking those who obeyed Aaron, leaving the Israelites, and joining Moses rather than remaining among them.
rows.anchor: وهذا قول ابن عباس في رواية عطاء

rows.speaker: مقاتل
rows.claim: Muqātil says Moses meant following his prior instruction to deputize him, reform the people, and avoid the corrupt; Aaron should have fought and disciplined them.
rows.anchor: فلم تركت قتالهم وتأديبهم وهذا قول مقاتل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rāzī says abandoning a commanded duty is disobedience deserving punishment; the threats in 72:23 and 4:14 together show that a command entails obligation.
rows.anchor: تارك المأمور به عاص والعاصي مستحق للعقاب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One explanation is that Aaron called Moses “son of my mother” to soften him and make him release his hold; another is that they literally shared a mother.
rows.anchor: قيل : إنما خاطبه بذلك ليدفعه عنه فيتركه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The prohibition does not prove Moses had actually seized Aaron: forbidding an act does not establish that it occurred, as in 33:48 and the conditional warning at 39:65.
rows.anchor: فإن النهي عن الشيء لا يدل على كون المنهي فاعلا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Even the stated act of pulling Aaron by the head does not show contempt; it could serve any of the other purposes Rāzī has described.
rows.anchor: والذي فيه أنه أخذ برأس أخيه يجره إليه وهذا القدر لا يدل على الاستخفاف به

rows.speaker: من الناس
rows.claim: Some say Moses took Aaron by the forelocks in his right hand and by the beard with his left.
rows.anchor: ومن الناس من يقول إنه أخذ ذؤابتيه بيمينه ولحيته بيساره

words: إِنِّى خَشِيتُ أَن تَقُولَ فَرَّقْتَ بَيْنَ بَنِىٓ إِسْرَٰٓءِيلَ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rāzī reconciles Aaron's answer with Moses' order by making the order conditional: Aaron should follow only if doing so would not cause disorder; joining Moses amid disorder would violate that condition.
rows.anchor: لعل موسى عليه السلام إنما أمره بالذهاب إليه بشرط أن لا يؤدي ذلك إلى فساد في القوم

rows.speaker: أبو القاسم الأنصاري
rows.claim: Abū al-Qāsim al-Anṣārī argues that divine guidance benefits more than signs: the magicians saw one sign, believed, and endured severe punishment without recanting.
rows.anchor: الهداية أنفع من الدلالة فإن السحرة كانوا أجانب عن الإيمان

rows.speaker: أبو القاسم الأنصاري
rows.claim: He contrasts the Israelites, who witnessed the staff-serpent, its swallowing the magicians' displays and return to a staff, the magicians' confession, nine signs, and the divided sea and deliverance, yet still sought idols.
rows.anchor: وأما قومه فإنهم رأوا انقلاب العصا ثعبانا والتقم كل ما جمعه السحرة ثم عاد عصا

rows.speaker: أبو القاسم الأنصاري
rows.claim: After crossing the sea, the Israelites asked for a god like the idolaters' and worshipped the calf when they heard its sound, showing that signs alone do not achieve faith without guidance.
rows.anchor: ثم إن هؤلاء مع ما شاهدوا من هذه الآيات لما خرجوا من البحر

rows.speaker: حمزة والكسائي
rows.claim: Ḥamza and al-Kisāʾī read “yā ibn ummi” with kasra and genitive construction, the kasra signaling the omitted yāʾ; the others read with fatḥa, understood as “yā ibn ummāh.”
rows.anchor: قرأ حمزة والكسائي : ( يا ابن أم ) بكسر الميم والإضافة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After consoling the Prophet about what people said and directing him to glorification, God follows with a prohibition against gazing at their worldly allotment.
rows.anchor: لما صبر رسوله عليه السلام على ما يقولون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One view takes this literally: prolonging the gaze means lingering in admiration without turning away; an ordinary brief glance followed by lowering the eyes is excused.
rows.anchor: المراد منه نظر العين وهؤلاء قالوا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rāzī illustrates the temptation with Qarun's spectators wishing for his fortune and the learned believers answering that God's reward is better for believers who act rightly.
rows.anchor: كما فعل نظارة قارون حيث قالوا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because gazing at worldly adornment is instinctive, the verse warns against a habitual lingering look; ascetics therefore urged lowering the eyes from tyrants' buildings and the clothes and mounts of the immoral, since spectators advance their display's purpose.
rows.anchor: ولما كان النظر إلى الزخارف كالمركوز في الطباع

rows.speaker: أبو مسلم
rows.claim: Abū Muslim says the prohibition concerns grief over what others received in worldly fortune, not looking at it.
rows.anchor: قال أبو مسلم الذي نهى عنه بقوله

rows.speaker: أبو رافع
rows.claim: Abū Rāfiʿ reports that after a guest came, the Prophet sent him to a Jew for a sale or loan; the Jew required collateral, so the Prophet sent his armor, and the verse was revealed.
rows.anchor: قال أبو رافع : ( نزل ضيف بالنبي صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: النبي
rows.claim: The Prophet said God does not look at people's forms or wealth, but at their hearts and deeds; Rāzī gives no grading.
rows.anchor: وقال عليه السلام : ( إن الله لا ينظر إلى صوركم ولا إلى أموالكم

rows.speaker: أبو الدرداء
rows.claim: Abū al-Dardāʾ calls the world a home for the homeless and wealth for the wealthless, gathered by those lacking reason.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو الدرداء : الدنيا دار من لا دار له

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan says that without people's foolishness, the world would be ruined.
rows.anchor: وعن الحسن : لولا حمق الناس لخربت الدنيا

rows.speaker: عيسى ابن مريم
rows.claim: Jesus son of Mary warns people not to take the world as a lord, lest it make them its slaves.
rows.anchor: وعن عيسى ابن مريم عليه السلام قال : لا تتخذوا الدنيا ربا

rows.speaker: عروة بن الزبير
rows.claim: When ʿUrwa ibn al-Zubayr saw what rulers possessed, he recited this verse and called people to prayer and God's mercy.
rows.anchor: وعن عروة بن الزبير أنه كان إذا رآى ما عند السلاطين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rāzī glosses “what We have given them to enjoy” as what We have made delightful: pleasing sights, melodies, scents, clothing, and sexual or marital pleasures.
rows.anchor: والإمتاع الإلذاذ بما يدرك من المناظر الحسنة ويسمع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He notes the forms “amtāʿan” and “mattāʿan”; the intensive tفعيل form suggests repeated or abundant enjoyment.
rows.anchor: يقال أمتعه إمتاعا ومتعه تمتيعا والتفعيل يقتضي التكثير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rāzī first explains “groups” as counterparts among the unbelievers: the word derives from pairing and resemblance, since they resemble one another in straying from right judgment.
rows.anchor: أي أشكالا وأشباها من الكفار وهي من المزاوجة بين الأشياء وهي المشاكلة

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās glosses “azwājan” as classes or kinds of people.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس رضي الله عنهما : أصنافا منهم

rows.speaker: الكلبي والزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Kalbī and al-Zajjāj gloss “azwājan” as men.
rows.anchor: وقال الكلبي والزجاج : رجالا منهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rāzī lists four accusative analyses for “zahra”: blame or specification; a second object if “We gave” is implied; apposition to the prepositional phrase's case; or apposition to “groups” with an implied “possessors of.”
rows.anchor: ففي انتصابه أربعة أوجه . أحدها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: For the vocalized form, Rāzī gives “zahra” its ordinary sense of adornment and brightness, as in “jahra” in the reading of 2:55.
rows.anchor: قلنا معنى الزهرة بعينه وهو الزينة والبهجة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, “zahra” may be a plural of “zāhir,” describing the worldly people as bright-faced and radiant, unlike the pale, plainly dressed righteous.
rows.anchor: وأن يكون جمع زاهر وصفا لهم بأنهم زهرة هذه الدنيا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One explanation of the test is punishment through wealth and children, as in the warning that God intends to punish people by them in worldly life.
rows.anchor: أحدها : لنعذبهم به كقوله

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās explains the test as God's causing them to go astray.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس رضي الله عنهما : إضلالا مني لهم

rows.speaker: الكبي ومقاتل
rows.claim: Al-Kalbī and Muqātil say worldly abundance intensifies obligation: resisting available pleasures is harder, the rich bear duties the poor lack, and those able to sin find abstention harder.
rows.anchor: قال الكبي ومقاتل تشديدا في التكاليف عليهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rāzī's preferred reading is that the reward the Prophet will receive is better than the unbelievers' worldly gain and endures, unlike their temporary possessions.
rows.anchor: والأظهر أن المراد أن مطلوبك الذي تجده من الثواب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another possibility is that even modest worldly provision joined with obedience is better in its outcome and more lasting, if one is content and patient with it.
rows.anchor: ويحتمل أن يكون المراد ما أوتيته من يسير الدنيا إذا قرنته بالطاعة خير لك من حيث العاقبة وأبقى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A further possibility is that “your Lord's provision” means the prophethood and exalted ranks given to the Prophet.
rows.anchor: ويحتمل أن يكون المراد ما أعطى من النبوة والدرجات الرفيعة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some take “your family” as relatives, but Rāzī prefers all followers of the Prophet's religion, paralleling 19:55; he also allows the household residents, whom he could remind of prayer at its times.
rows.anchor: وهذا أقرب وهو كقوله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rāzī allows “your family” to mean those who live in the house, since they can be reminded of the prayer at its appointed times; as God ordered the Prophet, he should order his people.
rows.anchor: وإن احتمل أن يكون المراد من يضمه المسكن إذ التنبيه على الصلاة والأمر بها في أوقاتها ممكن فيهم دون سائر الأمة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet should maintain prayer in practice as he commands it, since preaching by one's actions is more complete than preaching by words.
rows.anchor: فحافظ عليها فعلا ، فإن الوعظ بلسان الفعل أتم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rāzī reports that after this verse was revealed, the Prophet visited Fāṭima and ʿAlī every morning, called them to prayer, and continued for months.
rows.anchor: صلى الله عليه وسلم بعد نزول هذه الآية يذهب إلى فاطمة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rāzī says the command to pray serves people's benefit; God is above needing any benefit from their worship.
rows.anchor: ثم بين تعالى أنه إنما يأمرهم بذلك لمنافعهم وأنه متعال عن المنافع

rows.speaker: أبو مسلم
rows.claim: Abū Muslim says God seeks worship from the Prophet and people, not their provision as masters demand tribute from slaves, paralleling 51:56–57.
rows.anchor: قال أبو مسلم : المعنى أنه تعالى إنما يريد منه ومنهم العبادة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another explanation is that God does not ask the Prophet or his family to provide for themselves; God provides for them so he can devote his attention to the afterlife, as the saying goes, whoever works for God has God attend to his work.
rows.anchor: لنفسك ولا لأهلك بل نحن نرزقك ونرزق أهلك ، ففرغ بالك لأمر الآخرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A third explanation is that God gains nothing from the commanded prayer: He provides worldly blessings and hereafter reward instead.
rows.anchor: بل نحن نرزقك في الدنيا بوجوه النعم وفي الآخرة بالثواب

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن سلام
rows.claim: ʿAbd Allāh ibn Salām reports that whenever hardship or distress came upon the Prophet's family, he told them to pray and recited this verse.
rows.anchor: قال عبد الله بن سلام : ( كان النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse does not permit abandoning livelihood, since the pious are described as people whom trade and sale do not distract from remembering God.
rows.anchor: واعلم أنه ليس في الآية رخصة في ترك التكسب لأنه تعالى قال في وصف المتقين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The beautiful final outcome belongs to those who fear God.
rows.anchor: والعاقبة للتقوى فالمراد والعاقبة الجميلة لأهل التقوى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After the counsel on patience and prayer, Rāzī reads the following account of the opponents' objection as continuing the instruction to endure what they say in 20:130.
rows.anchor: ثم إنه سبحانه بعد هذه الوصية حكى عنهم شبهتهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The opponents' demand for a sign insinuates that they are being asked to believe without one; elsewhere they call the revelation confused dreams.
rows.anchor: أوهموا بهذا الكلام أنه يكلفهم الإيمان من غير آية

words: أَوَلَمْ تَأْتِهِم بَيِّنَةُ مَا فِى ٱلصُّحُفِ ٱلْأُولَىٰ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One explanation is that the Quran's agreement with earlier scriptures, though Muhammad had no schooling or teacher, conveyed unseen knowledge and was itself a miracle.
rows.anchor: أن ما في القرآن إذ وافق ما في كتبهم

words: أَوَلَمْ تَأْتِهِم بَيِّنَةُ مَا فِى ٱلصُّحُفِ ٱلْأُولَىٰ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A second explanation is that the earlier scriptures contain prophecies of Muhammad, his prophethood, and his mission.
rows.anchor: أن بينة ما في الصحف الأولى ما فيها من البشارة بمحمد صلى الله عليه وسلم وبنبوته وبعثته

words: أَوَلَمْ تَأْتِهِم بَيِّنَةُ مَا فِى ٱلصُّحُفِ ٱلْأُولَىٰ
rows.speaker: ابن جرير والقفال
rows.claim: Ibn Jarīr and al-Qaffāl say the proof is the Quran's account of earlier peoples destroyed after demanding signs and disbelieving, a warning that these questioners might meet the same fate.
rows.anchor: وثالثها : ذكر ابن جرير والقفال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The masculine pronoun referring back to the feminine “bayyina” is justified because “bayyina” has the masculine sense of proof or evidence.
rows.anchor: واعلم أنه إنما ذكر الضمير الراجع إلى البينة لأنها في معنى البرهان والدليل

words: وَلَوْ أَنَّا أَهْلَكْنَٰهُم بِعَذَابٍۢ مِّن قَبْلِهِۦ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Before sending the Messenger, destruction would have given them an excuse to ask why no messenger was sent; after his message clarified duties and rights, they have no excuse and the proof is against them.
rows.anchor: فأما الآن وقد أرسلناك وبينا على لسانك لهم ما عليهم وما لهم فلا حجة لهم البتة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Before it” can mean before the Messenger was sent or before the signs God manifested.
rows.anchor: يحتمل من قبل إرساله ويحتمل من قبل ما أظهره من البينات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although the destroyed cannot speak, Rāzī says the verse means they would have had a claim on Judgment Day; the mention of humiliation and disgrace fits the punishment of the afterlife.
rows.anchor: قلنا المعنى لكان لهم أن يقولوا ذلك يوم القيامة

rows.speaker: النبي
rows.claim: Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī reports the Prophet's account of three who plead on Judgment Day: a person from the interval without a messenger, the cognitively impaired, and a child. A fire is raised; those destined for misery enter and the blessed remain, then God says their refusal foretells how they would have treated messengers. Rāzī gives no grading.
rows.anchor: قال عليه السلام : ( يحتج على الله تعالى يوم القيامة ثلاثة

rows.speaker: القاضي
rows.claim: Al-Qāḍī criticizes the report, arguing that punishment is not appropriate for someone who lacks rational capacity.
rows.anchor: والقاضي طعن في الخبر وقال : لا يحسن العقاب على من لا يعقل
